newsitem.title: CANADA: GM, union dig in for long strike over outsourcing.
newsitem.headline: GM, union dig in for long strike over outsourcing.

text.p: With more than 21,000 workers on strike and another 5,000 set to join them Wednesday night, the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union and General Motors Corp. appear to be digging in for a long strike.
Neither side has shown any sign of budging in the stand-off that started on Oct. 3 when the CAW began a series of strikes with a walkout at GM plants in Oshawa, Ontario.

The dispute has centered on GM's ability to shift work to outside, usually non-union companies -- a practice known as outsourcing -- that would cut 5,500 union jobs at its Canadian operations. Wages and work rules have also been at issue.
CAW President Buzz Hargrove and GM Canada lead negotiator Dean Munger have continued to meet daily, but Hargrove said the meetings usually deteriorate into shouting matches.

With the strike in its sixth day Tuesday, GM plants in the United States have been running short of some components made in Canada and told workers to stay home for the second straight day. GM's suppliers in Canada were also affected.
GM Canada spokesman Stew Low would not speculate on how long the strike would drag on. "The issue is very serious and we just have to work on it as long as we can," Low said.
Some analysts said the world's largest automaker will try to wait out the strike, hoping to deplete the union's $37 million strike fund.
"They will go as long as it takes," one analyst said in Toronto.

But Hargrove said the union's strike fund could last at least 12 weeks and stretch to 16 weeks if new credit is arranged. The CAW also has set a special meeting for Oct. 18 to raise funds from all its 210,000 members across Canada.
All 26,000 CAW members at GM will be on strike as of Wednesday under the union's escalating strike plan.
"GM can't out wait us," Hargrove said. "We're not going anywhere."
Analysts said GM did not want to give in to the CAW while negotiations continued with the United Auto Workers (UAW) union in the United States.
"They (GM) are not about to give Canada (workers) a relatively generous deal while they are negotiating in the U.S.," said Denis Desrosier, president of Desrosier Automotive Consultants Inc.

A brief strike in Canada would be cheaper for GM than a UAW settlement based on what Hargrove wants for CAW workers, he said. If GM settled with the CAW first, it would encourage the UAW to seek a similar contract.
GM has said it needs more flexibility to outsource work to remain competitive with Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp.
Desrosier said GM has about $13 billion in cash and could afford a strike in Canada that he estimated would cost GM up to $35 million a week.
Other analysts have said the strike in Canada could cost GM as much as $150 million a week.
Desrosier said the CAW probably will get the deal it wants after UAW President Stephen Yokich settles with GM in the United States.
"I guarantee you Buzz (Hargrove) is going to be a winner, but it's going to come after the (United) States," Desrosier said.
Hargrove said that after the rest of GM workers join the strike, the union will decide whether to start negotiating with Ford Motor Co..
In September, the CAW signed an industry pattern deal with Chrysler Corp., which banned the sale or closing of any plants and committed the automaker to replace any jobs lost to outsourcing.
Traditionally, the CAW reaches a contract with one of the Big Three North American automakers and then applies that deal to the other two.
